fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

fundamental.thesis: Kotak Mahindra Bank is one of India's largest private-sector banks, with a strong capital base (CET1 22.1%) and growing wealth and asset-management arms (customer AUM ₹8.14L cr, +8% YoY). Profit growth has picked up sharply: consolidated PAT rose 26.3% YoY to ₹5,645 cr in Q2FY27, up from +23.0% in Q1FY27 and +5.0% in Q3FY26, and standalone NII rose 16% to ₹8,459 cr. Asset quality has improved steadily, with GNPA falling from 1.39% to 1.04% over five periods and slippages down 24%, but this quarter's growth comes partly off a weak base (Q2FY26 PAT was -2.7%), and NIM fell 23bps YoY to 4.31% as costlier FCNR(B) deposits came in. On the bank yardstick (P/B plus ROE, not P/E), a P/B of 2.08x against an ROE of only 11.4-11.7% is fair, not cheap; it sits at the 86th percentile among bank peers on both P/B and forward P/E (13.6x), so it already carries a premium that its current ROE does not clearly earn. The biggest risk is margin squeeze: falling NIM, CASA slipping from 42.3% to 41.8%, a 4.52% cost of funds and an 8.1% cut to next-FY EPS estimates while 32 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a re-rating lower.

Titan is India's largest organised jewellery retailer (Tanishq), with watches, eyecare and the newly consolidated Damas (Gulf) business, and it gains from the premiumisation trend. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 19.1% YoY to ₹41,970 cr and reported PAT rose 88.6% to ₹4,170 cr (9.9% margin). That profit includes a ₹671 cr one-off fair-value gain on the Damas put option, so underlying PAT is about ₹3,499 cr: +58% YoY on an 8.3% margin. Part of the revenue growth comes from the Damas acquisition rather than the existing business. We only have this one half-year period with no standalone Q2 or prior-quarter rows, so the quarter-by-quarter trend cannot be checked. We used peer P/E and EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for premium discretionary names, and the stock is expensive on both: trailing P/E 74.3x (forward 49.4x) is inside the card's 60-100x range for premium names but 87% above the sector median of 39.7x, and EV/EBITDA of 48.1x sits at the 94th percentile, more than double the 21.9x peer median. Sell-side estimates have been raised 7% over 90 days, which supports earnings delivery but leaves little room for disappointment at around 72% of the 52-week range. The biggest worry is cash: operating cash flow was -₹11,177 cr against positive PAT, borrowings rose 2.5x to ₹24,265 cr, and inventory reached ₹50,861 cr.

fundamental.thesis: Bank of Baroda is one of India's largest public-sector banks, with about ₹15L cr of advances. Domestic loans grew 13.5% and international loans grew 39.7%. Q2FY27 total income rose 19.8% YoY to ₹41,966 cr and net profit rose 35.8% YoY to ₹6,532 cr, a PAT margin of 15.6%. The jump came after a very weak Q1FY27 (PAT of ₹1,278–1,783 cr; the sources disagree), so H1FY27 profit is still down 16.5% YoY. The underlying picture is mixed: asset quality is improving (GNPA fell from 1.99% to 1.78%, NNPA from 0.50% to 0.37%, provision coverage is 94.7%), but net interest margin keeps slipping (2.89% in FY26, 2.77% in Q1, 2.74% in Q2), CASA fell to 36.4% and fee income fell 8.5%. That suggests treasury gains and lower costs drove part of the Q2 beat, not core lending spread. For a lender I graded valuation on price-to-book against return on equity, not P/E: at 0.81x book with a 12.7% trailing ROE (19.3% annualised in Q2), the stock is cheap in absolute terms and against peers. It ranks P7 on P/B (median 1.5x) and P21 on trailing P/E (6.8x vs a 16.8x peer median). Part of that discount is the usual PSU-bank discount, so cheap here does not mean mispriced. The biggest risk is that margins keep sliding while credit costs rise (0.55% vs 0.29% a year ago), making the Q2 profit spike a one-off rather than the new run-rate. Data caveats: the Q3FY26 and H1FY26 rows in the trend table look like a much smaller entity (deposits ₹1.5L cr), so the pre-computed trajectory signals are unreliable. Live data also has errors (a 322% dividend yield, and the 52-week position does not match the price implied by the analyst target), so I lowered conviction.

The forward P/E of 23.3x is higher than trailing (P38, about 9% below the peer median), EV/EBITDA is 16.1x (P31), and the stock trades at 90% of its 52-week range, so overall it is fair rather than clearly cheap. The biggest risk is that the US generics business keeps shrinking or faces a tariff, at the same time as MedTech integration losses (-29% segment margin) keep weighing on earnings.

fundamental.thesis: IDFC First Bank is a mid-sized private bank with a retail-heavy loan book and a strong deposit franchise (CASA 48.4%), now scaling fast after years of rebuilding profitability. In Q2FY27, PAT was ₹1,045 cr, up 196.5% YoY off a depressed base and above ₹1,000 cr for a second straight quarter. Loans grew 30.1% YoY (22.2% excluding FCNR(B)-backed loans, up from 20.6% in Q1), deposits grew 25.9%, and asset quality kept improving: net NPA fell from 0.48% to 0.44% to 0.40%, and gross NPA was 1.32% vs 1.61% at FY26-end. Valuation is graded on P/B plus ROE, as the sector card requires for lenders, not on trailing P/E: P/B is 1.31x (P36 among peers, 11% below the 1.5x median) against annualised ROE of only 10.6%, which is below the 12% bar for 'cheap', so the stock is fair. The 38x trailing P/E is distorted by weak FY26 earnings (PAT ₹1,611 cr), and the 11x forward P/E sits exactly at the peer median. The main risk is that rapid growth is outpacing the bank's profitability engine: CASA slipped from 50.8% to 48.4% and NIM was diluted by FCNR(B) funding, Q2 ROA fell to 0.93% from 1.06%, and capital adequacy (CAR) dropped to 15.05% from 15.6% while the loan book grows about 30%.

fundamental.thesis: Punjab National Bank is India's second-largest public-sector lender, with ₹13.4 lakh crore of advances that grew 14.7% YoY, led by MSME (+19.8%) and overseas loans (+62.7%). In Q2 FY27, total income rose 5.4% YoY to ₹38,185 cr and net profit rose 12.8% to ₹5,532 cr; asset quality keeps improving, with Gross NPA down from 3.19% to 2.95% to 2.55%, Net NPA at 0.25%, slippage at 0.77% and provision coverage at 97%, though the revenue trend is noisy because one period row looks inconsistent. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, the stock trades at 0.83x book against a 13% TTM ROE (17.3% in the latest quarter), which is about 44% below the regional-bank median P/B of 1.5x and in the bottom 15% of peers, so it grades as cheap; the trailing P/E of 6.75x is consistent with that but is not the main yardstick. The main concern is funding: cost of deposits rose from 2.50% to 2.74% YoY, CASA slipped from 37.0% to 36.6%, domestic deposits grew only 9.5% against 12.5% domestic loan growth, and treasury income fell 57%, all of which could cap the 2.6–2.7% margin guidance.

GAIL is India's largest gas transmission and marketing company. Gas marketing produced about 56% of segment profit in H1 (₹7,131 cr), regulated pipelines added ₹3,964 cr at a 58% margin, and petrochemicals lost ₹168 cr. Growth was very strong in H1 FY27: revenue rose 24.7% to ₹88,651 cr and PAT rose 115% to ₹9,395 cr. Q2 looks even faster, with implied revenue of about ₹47,300 cr (roughly +33% YoY, against +16.7% in Q1). By the press-release figures, Q2 revenue was ₹45,924 cr and PAT ₹4,650 cr, a margin of about 10.1%, down from 11.3% in Q1. The pre-computed trend signals mix half-year and quarter periods, so I did not rely on them. Using enterprise value to operating profit (EV/EBITDA) plus dividend yield, as the sector card advises for a volume and tariff business, valuation is fair. EV/EBITDA is 11.6x, exactly the peer median, and trailing P/E is 14.65x, at the peer median and just above the 8–14x energy range. P/B is 1.26x against an annualised H1 ROE of about 19%, which looks attractive. The forward P/E of 9.5x depends on FY27 estimates that analysts raised 28% in 30 days while trimming next-year estimates by 3.5%. The biggest risk is that the doubling of profit comes mostly from gas-marketing spreads, which swing with LNG prices and are not structural. That makes FY27 look like a peak year. The newly started Mangalore PTA plant (purified terephthalic acid, a petrochemical) also adds exposure to a segment that is currently losing money.

fundamental.thesis: Muthoot Finance is India's largest gold-loan NBFC. It benefits from lower interest rates, which cut its borrowing costs, and from high gold prices, which let it lend more against the same gold. In Q1 FY27 total income was ₹8,695 cr, up 34.5% year on year, and profit (PAT) was ₹2,825 cr, up 43.1%. Q2, worked out from the H1 totals, was about ₹9,788 cr income and ₹3,221 cr PAT, a 32.9% margin. Growth is still very strong but slowing: income growth has eased from +58% (9M FY26) to +34.5% (Q1 FY27), loan book growth from about 51% to 43%, and PAT margin from 36.2% to roughly 33%. For a lender the right valuation test is price-to-book against return on equity. A P/B of 3.04x looks fair for a 30% ROE and sits right at the peer median, so we grade it fair, not cheap. The P/E of 11.2x (8.6x forward) is 44% below the peer median, so a cheap case is possible if the 30% ROE holds after gold prices stop rising. The main risks are that gold, now falling from its highs, could slow loan growth and squeeze loan-to-value headroom, and the open GST search under Section 67 of the CGST Act, disclosed on 2026-11-02.

fundamental.thesis: Aurobindo Pharma is a large Indian generics maker that earns 92% of its revenue abroad, including 44% from the US and 31% from Europe; 89% of revenue comes from finished medicines and 11% from APIs (the active drug ingredients). Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹10,263 cr, up 23.9% YoY, and profit after tax (PAT) was ₹1,124 cr, up 32.5%, a sharp pickup from +6–8% growth in Q3–Q4 FY26. PAT margin edged up to about 11.0% from 10.5%, but part of this jump comes from buying Lannett, a US generics company consolidated from June 29, 2026, so the underlying organic growth is unclear, especially after US revenue fell 13% in Q4 FY26. On valuation I relied mainly on EV/EBITDA and checked it against peers: EV/EBITDA is 12.0x against a peer median of 21.4x, P/E is 24.0x against the 28–40x sector range and P15 among peers, and forward P/E of 16.4x is the cheapest in its peer group (P0), so the stock is cheap, though part of that discount reflects a lower ROE of 9.9% and heavy US generics exposure. Some snapshot figures look wrong: a 27% dividend yield, debt/equity of 21x when the company reports net cash of $189M, and a consensus target that does not match the 52-week range. The biggest risk is the US: if the review of generics in US tariff policy goes against Indian makers, or Lannett's integration slips, earnings could fall, and the stock is already near the top of its 52-week range.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Bank is a mid-sized public-sector bank with a ₹8.74L cr deposit base and ₹7.11L cr of advances, and about two-thirds of its loans go to retail, agriculture and MSME borrowers (RAM 65%). Stripping it out, underlying PAT growth looks closer to high single digits, and the core trend is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 2.23% to 1.86% to 1.61% with PCR at 98%. Against that, NIM slipped from 3.37% to 3.24%, credit cost rose from 0.21% to 0.47% to 0.71% over three quarters, and deposits are growing slower than loans (12.5% vs 17.5% YoY). Using P/B against ROE (the lender yardstick), 1.44x book for a 15.4% ROE is cheap in absolute terms, but peers are similar: P/B is only at P43 and P/E (9.9x) at P29 among regional banks, so the grade is fair. Analysts raised FY EPS estimates by about 5% over 90 days, which supports the case. The main risk is that loans keep growing faster than deposits, pushing up funding costs and squeezing NIMs further just as credit costs rise.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics company that sells mainly chronic-therapy medicines. Its revenue comes from branded generics in India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%) plus US generics (29%), and it ranks #1 in India in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 Indian pharma companies (IQVIA, MAT Sep-26). Growth is speeding up: quarterly revenue growth went from +14% in Q2FY26 to +20% in Q3FY26, +24.8% in Q1FY27 and about +33% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr). Q2 profit after tax rose 49% to ₹388 cr (a 21.6% margin), and H1FY27 revenue of ₹3,420 cr (+28.8%) and PAT of ₹722 cr (+39.9%) show margins widening from 19.0% to 21.1% over the period. Using pharma P/E plus peer rank as the yardstick, the trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28–40x sector range and right at the peer median (46th percentile), and the forward P/E of 26.3x builds in more growth, so the stock is fair rather than cheap; it is above the peer median on P/B (77th percentile) and EV/EBITDA (69th percentile), and it trades at 68% of its 52-week range. The biggest risks are the 29% of revenue from US generics, which faces the pending US Commerce review of generics, and the fact that margins are quoted 'adjusted' for forex losses while cash conversion is only about 0.85x profit, so earnings quality needs watching.

fundamental.thesis: City Union Bank is a mid-sized private bank with 1,002 branches, and its loan book of about ₹72,442 cr has grown well ahead of the roughly 16% system credit growth cited for FY26. In Q2 FY27, PAT rose 27% YoY to ₹416 cr, net interest income rose 31% to ₹873 cr, advances rose 26% and deposits rose 21%, while gross NPA improved from 2.17% (9M FY26) to 1.91% (FY26) to 1.44% (H1 FY27); however, the table's accelerating and margin-expansion signals are unreliable because the FY26 revenue row (₹2,830 cr) looks wrong and Q2 revenue has no YoY figure, so the firmer evidence is the implied sequential rise in PAT from about ₹382 cr to ₹416 cr. Headline revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +34.6% in Q1FY26 to +3.8% in Q1FY27, and is about +7.3% in Q2FY27 (₹7,004 cr, derived as H1 minus Q1). Margins are moving the other way: Q2FY27 PAT of about ₹291 cr is up about 21% YoY, H1 PAT of ₹603 cr is up 34%, PBT margin rose 130 bps to 6.1%, and net debt fell 98% to ₹72 cr, earning a AA+ credit rating. The main risk is that slow revenue conversion, together with a weak cash-flow history (Q2FY26 free cash flow of -₹826 cr), points to execution or working-capital strain across a very large and complex project backlog.

On valuation I used EV/EBITDA plus P/B with ROE, the right yardsticks for a capital-intensive shipping company. EV/EBITDA is 4.7x, near the bottom of the broad market (P2). P/B is 1.19x against an 18.8% ROE, and trailing P/E is 6.9x, all cheap. However, shipping stocks normally trade at low multiples near peak freight rates. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/E against low-margin distribution peers, not the Industrials or IT-services medians. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 14.3x, forward P/E 10.1x, EV/EBITDA 9.4x and P/B 2.1x with ROE of 13.1%, all in the bottom 10–20% of the broad market. fundamental.thesis: Gland Pharma is a mid-cap injectables maker: it develops and manufactures injectable drugs for partners (B2B) and makes them to order for other drug companies (CDMO). It sells mainly into the US, where Q1 FY27 revenue rose 32% YoY to ₹981 cr, and owns the European CDMO Cenexi. In Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹1,800 cr, up 20% YoY, and PAT was ₹317 cr, up 47% YoY, for a PAT margin of 17.6%. Revenue growth has picked up from +6–7% a year ago to +20–23% over the last three quarters, and PAT margin has widened from 12–14% to about 18%, though revenue grew only 3% and PAT fell 14% versus Q4. Using the pharma P/E yardstick, a trailing P/E of 35.3x is inside the 28–40x sector range and at the median of its broad-market peers (P50). EV/EBITDA of 20.1x and P/B of 3.5x are below the peer median, and the forward P/E of 24.1x prices in continued growth, so overall valuation is fair, not cheap. The stock also sits at 76% of its 52-week range. Management raised its medium-term growth target to about 20% CAGR from 15% and estimates are up 5–7% over 90 days, but the biggest risks are that the strong US growth slows (the US is reviewing whether generic drugs should also face tariffs) and an overhang from a promoter-side Fosun shareholding disclosure that arrived alongside a board change, ahead of Q2 results on 6 Nov.

LG Electronics India is a leading consumer-durables maker in India. Home appliances (ACs, refrigerators, washing machines) bring in about 88% of revenue at a thin 9.4% segment margin, and home entertainment brings in about 12% at a much richer 38.9% margin. The business is speeding up: H1 FY27 revenue rose 17.4% YoY to ₹14,613 cr and PAT rose 26.5% to ₹1,142 cr. The implied Q2 (H1 minus Q1) shows revenue of about ₹7,380 cr (+19% YoY) and PAT of about ₹489 cr (+26% YoY), continuing a recovery in revenue growth from -6.4% to +8.1%, then +15.5%, then about +19% over the last four quarters. Earnings are backed by cash (CFO/PAT 1.43x) and the company holds ₹4,569 cr of net cash. The reported 5.99 debt/equity looks like a units error, since the only debt is ₹482 cr of lease liabilities. On valuation, the stock trades at 64.8x trailing P/E, 41.2x forward P/E and 42.5x EV/EBITDA. That puts it in the top quintile of the broad market (P81–P92; no tight durables peers were available), but inside the 60–100x premium band the sector card treats as normal for consumer discretionary. With earnings growing about 25% and a forward P/E of 41x, I grade it fair, not cheap, and the stock sits at 68% of its 52-week range. The main risk is the board-approved move into automotive electronics: it consumed ₹1,163 cr of capex in H1 and the company has given no financial targets for it. Together with price competition in appliances and rising crude feeding into input costs, this could dilute returns on equity (ROE, currently 24.7%) and squeeze margins.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a PSU mid-cap refinery (ONGC subsidiary) processing ~4.4 MMT/quarter of crude at Mangalore, operating in a policy-administered margin environment where GRMs, not crude price alone, drive earnings. H1FY27 revenue surged +67.6% YoY to ₹77,199 cr and PAT exploded +697.6% YoY to ₹2,846 cr (PAT margin 3.7%), a dramatic recovery from the near-zero-profit FY26 base (PAT margin 1.8%), with EBITDA margin expanding to 6.6% on strong throughput and higher product realisations — though a fire incident at the CHT unit on 30-Sep-2026 provisionally cost ₹118 cr and creates near-term operational uncertainty. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive refinery (per sector card guidance for PSU OMCs/refiners), MRPL trades at 5.97× EV/EBITDA versus a broad-market median of 23.3× — placing it at P3 in its peer universe — making it structurally cheap, though the sector card explicitly cautions this discount is 'policy-priced' (permanent policy risk, not a valuation error); trailing P/E of 14.5× sits at the upper end of the PSU OMC range (6–10× + yield), but the forward P/E collapses to 3.4×, implying the street is pricing in a very strong FY27 full-year earnings recovery. The key risk is that elevated crude at $97.97/bbl directly compresses refining marketing margins for OMC-adjacent refiners, estimate revisions are sharply negative (-9.6% 30d, -21.2% next-FY 90d) signalling analyst concern about GRM sustainability, and the CHT fire adds operational/insurance settlement uncertainty over the next 1–2 quarters.

ACME Solar is a mid-sized renewable power producer (IPP) with 2,990 MW running and about 5,080 MW under construction, and its 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs) are mostly with central-government buyers like NTPC. Such a company grows through new capacity and the spread between its returns and its cost of debt, and the new BESS (battery storage) and FDRE (round-the-clock renewable) projects are its growth engine. H1 FY27 revenue rose 78.2% YoY to ₹1,745 cr and PAT rose 105% to ₹504 cr. YoY growth has sped up from +59% (FY26) to +63% (Q1) to +78% (H1), and PAT margin rose from 19.9% to 24.7% to 28.9%. Within H1, the September quarter works out to roughly ₹791 cr revenue (below Q1, which fits the monsoon dip in solar output) but higher PAT of about ₹269 cr. Operating capacity barely moved in Q1 (+3.5% YoY), so near-term growth now depends on commissioning, which has started: 66.68 MW of solar plus BESS units went live in early November, and a 400 MW FDRE PPA was signed with NTPC. Valuation is fair: I graded it on EV/EBITDA, the card's yardstick for capital-heavy businesses. At 15.2x it is about 35% below the market median (P26), and the forward P/E of 13.7x is far below the trailing 40.7x, which suggests earnings growth is expected. But P/B of 4.0x against a 10.4% ROE is not cheap, and the stock sits at 80% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt/equity is about 3.9x, interest coverage is only 2.47x, finance costs take about 40% of EBITDA, and H1 free cash flow was -₹5,263 cr on ₹6,329 cr of capex. Grid connection delays (substations delivered on time only 60% of the time, about 6 months late on average) or higher interest rates could hold back the earnings ramp.

fundamental.thesis: CESC is a West Bengal-regulated power utility with a coal mine and other power operations, and its earnings depend heavily on tariff orders and regulatory income. In FY26, revenue rose 9.2% to Rs 18,570 cr and PAT rose 12.6% to Rs 1,542 cr, but no reliable filing data is available after FY26, and the trend signals mix annual and part-year periods, so I cannot confirm whether growth is speeding up or slowing down. Valuation is fair on EV/EBITDA of 10.92x, supported by a trailing P/E of 14.68x inside the 10-18x utilities range and P/B of 1.81x for 12.5% ROE; I gave little weight to the cheap broad-market peer rank because it does not compare utilities, and I ignored the 348% dividend yield, the +59.7% target upside (which does not fit the roughly Rs 170 price implied by the market cap and EPS) and the -100% estimate revisions as likely data errors. The biggest risk is that net debt of Rs 15,747 cr (4.44x EBITDA) and a 0.9 current ratio leave little cushion if regulatory income, already down from Rs 1,249 cr to Rs 903 cr, keeps falling or pending tariff appeals go against the company, and the results due from the 5 November board meeting could quickly change this view.

Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, Chennai-based vehicle-finance NBFC. Its group also includes housing finance, an asset manager and a general-insurance joint venture, and it is known for some of the best asset quality in its peer set. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 show standalone quarterly PAT of ₹475 cr (+21% YoY), H1FY27 consolidated PAT of ₹1,153 cr (+20%), disbursements up 28% YoY in Q2 (H1 +25%) and core lending AUM up 19% to ₹65,992 cr. Gross Stage 3 improved to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rose to 51% from 45%. One caution is that Q2 profit from operations grew only 11%, so part of the profit growth is coming from lower credit costs rather than core earnings; the pre-computed 'margin contracting' signal comes from mixed revenue bases and is not meaningful. On the lender yardstick (P/B against sustainable ROE), P/B of 3.5x against ROE of 16.75% (up from 15.9%) is fair to slightly rich: the stock is at P67 on P/B and P100 on forward P/E within its credit-services peer group, though the cheapest peers are the state-owned power lenders PFC and REC, a lower-quality comparison set. The biggest near-term risk is the chairman's resignation announced alongside results, alongside a capital adequacy ratio that slipped to 18.5% from 19.3% and a ₹66 cr Motor TP claims provision at Royal Sundaram after the Supreme Court judgment.

drivers: Management tone constructive but no formal guidance: 'steady sustainable growth' and 'outlook optimistic on domestic auto and financial services'. Results backed it up: consolidated PAT +20% to Rs. 1,153 cr, Q2 disbursements +28% YoY, AUM +19%

Concerns: capital adequacy fell from 19.3% to 18.5%, and Royal Sundaram's PAT more than halved after a Rs. 66 cr motor third-party claims provision following the Supreme Court ruling

technical.setup: Bounce inside a long-term downtrend: price has recovered above SMA20 (4,080) with MACD turning bullish, but it is still below a falling SMA50 (4,375) and SMA200 (4,640) in a death-cross structure, it lags both Nifty and its peers, and in the current mean-reverting market this looks like a relief rally into resistance rather than a confirmed pullback-to-support entry.

trader.reasoning: We are not buying today because the three analysts disagree. Q2FY27 results were solid (profit up 21%, loan disbursements up 28%, bad loans down) and the market liked them. But the valuation looks only fair, at 3.5x book value against a 16.75% return on equity. Underlying operating profit grew just 11%, so part of the profit jump came from setting aside less for bad loans. The chairman's sudden resignation alongside the results also adds governance and succession risk, which matters more for a midcap. On the charts, the stock is still in a downtrend below its falling 50-day and 200-day averages, and right now rallies like this have been fading rather than continuing. So we wait with no position. We would look again if the stock pulls back and holds near ₹4,080 (its 20-day average) or clearly breaks above ₹4,375 once there is more clarity on leadership.

drivers: Q2FY27 management tone: 'Margins at bottom in Q2; trajectory will be upward from Q3 onwards', helped by the October rate hike repricing about 70% of floating-rate loans by December. Deposits grew 18.8% YoY and retail disbursements rose to ₹90,000 cr from ₹76,000 cr.

Main risks: NIM is at a cycle low of 3.32%, and LCR is 113%, near the bottom of its 110–120% target range. The reported Q2 PAT of ₹1,950 cr looks inconsistent with the bank's size and should be checked against the results filing.
The market's results-day reaction was IN-LINE but slightly negative (-2.3% over 1–2 days), so it does not confirm management's optimism.

fundamental.thesis: HDFC Bank is India's largest private-sector bank, with ₹33.2L cr of deposits, ₹33.2L cr of advances and 9,706 branches, and its asset quality is very clean: GNPA is 1.11%, down from 1.15% at FY26-end, net NPA is 0.37% and credit cost is 44 bps. On volume, Q2FY27 deposits grew +18.8% YoY and advances grew +16.3%, but profitability is moving the wrong way. Management calls the 3.32% NIM a cycle low, ROA has fallen from 1.9% in FY26 to 1.48% in H1FY27, and H1 PAT of ₹35,869 cr is down -10.2% YoY on revenue down -4.1%, a 14.3% PAT margin. The ₹1,950 cr Q2 PAT figure (+12.7%) looks like an extraction error, and 30-day and 90-day FY EPS estimates have both been cut 5.6%. Using the lender yardstick of P/B against ROE, 1.98x book on a 13.8% TTM ROE (12.1% in H1) is fair in absolute terms, but it ranks P79 among bank peers on P/B even though P/E sits at the peer median of 16.8x. The stock is at 8.6% of its 52-week range, which helps the entry but does not make it cheap. The biggest risk is an abrupt leadership change: a new MD/CEO effective immediately and the Deputy MD retiring by December. This comes with a loan-to-deposit ratio near 100%, LCR tight at 113%, and a 25 bps October rate hike that management expects to reprice the 70% floating book upward, which conflicts with the sector card's easing-cycle prior.

Reliance is a conglomerate with four main businesses: oil refining and chemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (now listed separately as JPL), retail (RRVL) and new energy. Per the sector card it should be valued business by business (sum of the parts), not as a pure oil company. In Q2FY27 gross revenue was a record ₹362,268 cr, up 27.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹29,550 cr, up 33.8% YoY. Revenue growth has picked up from about -8.5% in FY26 to +24.5% in Q1 and +27.8% in Q2, and PAT margin improved from 6.8% in Q1 to 8.2%. However, much of this growth came from O2C, whose EBITDA rose 67.9% because fuel margins spiked on Middle East supply disruption. Retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%, and only Jio is growing steadily (revenue +11.4%, monthly ARPU ₹218.8). We have no sum-of-the-parts data, so as a fallback we used EV/EBITDA of 12.2x and trailing P/E of 21.7x. These look expensive next to the PSU energy peers (median 9.2x P/E, 6.1x EV/EBITDA), but those peers are policy-priced single businesses and not a fair yardstick for a conglomerate. With forward P/E at 18.0x, earnings estimates raised 15-21% over the last 30 days and the price near its 52-week low, we grade valuation fair, not expensive. The biggest risk is that record O2C margins are a temporary geopolitical windfall while retail and media are shrinking, at a time when ROE is only 9.1% and finance costs are up 24.2%.

fundamental.thesis: SBIN is India's largest bank, with a ₹78.9 trillion balance sheet, and its loan book is still growing fast: advances rose 17.8% YoY in Q2FY27, with SME up 22% and agri up 22.6%. Q2FY27 total income was ₹1,51,084 cr (+8.2% YoY), slightly faster than Q1's +7.8%. PAT was ₹23,038 cr (+14.3%), but one-off gains flatter that figure: ₹6,879 cr from selling part of SBI Funds Management in the consolidated results, plus NSE/ARCIL stake-sale gains booked to reserves. Core quality is mixed. Gross NPA improved from 1.49% to 1.39% and credit cost fell to 0.22%, but whole-bank margin (NIM) slipped from 3.03% to 2.94% and the share of low-cost deposits (CASA) fell from 39.5% to 38.3%. Valuation is judged on price-to-book against return on equity, as the sector card says to for banks: at 1.53x book with 15.5% trailing ROE (18.7% annualised this quarter), the stock is fair, close to cheap, sits at the 57th percentile of its peers on P/B, and is mid-range at 45% of its 52-week band.

fundamental.thesis: ITC is a conglomerate whose profits still come mainly from cigarettes, with FMCG, paper, agri and hotels-adjacent businesses around it; the sector card notes it trades on its own conglomerate multiple backed by dividends, so it should not be read as a pure FMCG name. Q2FY27 is the second quarter of a sharp profit decline after an unprecedented cigarette tax increase: consolidated revenue grew only +5% YoY, while implied Q2 PAT of about ₹4,229 cr (H1 ₹8,738 cr minus Q1 ₹4,509 cr) fell roughly -16% YoY, after -15.6% in Q1, against PAT growth of +1% to +3% through FY26. Cigarette net revenue fell -21% and segment results fell -27%, which drove consolidated EBITDA down -16%; non-cigarette businesses offset part of this, with EBITDA up +22%, FMCG Others revenue up +19% (a 14-quarter high) with margins up 50 bps, and paper PBIT up +48%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA plus peer rank because ITC is a conglomerate: at 12.1x EV/EBITDA and 16.9x trailing P/E it is the cheapest of 13 FMCG peers on every multiple (around 60-67% below the sector median of 51.5x P/E), near its 52-week low, and cash conversion has improved (CFO/PAT 0.96x vs 0.59x a year ago), so it is cheap. The cheapness looks like a tax-driven structural de-rating rather than a mispricing, and analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (FY EPS -4.8% over 90 days), so the multiple may stay low until cigarette volumes stabilise.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Unilever is India's largest FMCG company, with leading brands across home care, personal care and foods. Revenue growth sped up from +10.1% YoY in Q1FY27 to +14.5% in Q2FY27 (₹18,226 cr). Profit did not follow: PAT was flat at ₹2,790 cr (+0.3% YoY, after -3.2% in Q1), so PAT margin shrank from 17.5% a year ago to 15.3%. We also have no volume-growth figure for Q2; the last reported figure was 6% for Q4FY26, so we can't tell how much of the 14.5% is real demand and how much is price or mix. On P/E, the standard yardstick for FMCG, the stock trades at 46.6x trailing and 39.4x forward, inside the 40-60x sector range and only slightly above the peer median of 43.8x (P60 in its sector; P80 on forward P/E and EV/EBITDA), so we grade it fair. Being near its 52-week low gives some comfort on entry price, but it is not a bargain. The biggest risk is that sales keep growing while profit stays flat, which suggests input costs or extra spending are eating the gains.

fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

fundamental.thesis: UltraTech is India's largest cement maker with 210.1 mtpa of global grey capacity, and together with Adani it controls about 45% of industry capacity, which supports pricing discipline. Q2FY27 revenue rose 18.9% YoY to ₹23,024 cr and PAT rose 21.3% to ₹1,501 cr, with revenue growth accelerating from +15.8% in Q1, on 12.9% volume growth and EBITDA per tonne of ₹974 (+₹60 YoY, inside the ₹900–1,100 healthy band). The weak 6.5% PAT margin and the drop in EBITDA per tonne from ₹1,214 in Q1 mostly reflect the monsoon quarter, though fuel (+14%) and packing-bag (+30%) costs are rising with crude. The preferred cement yardstick, EV/EBITDA, was unavailable, so I graded on peers: a trailing P/E of 39.6x sits near the Materials peer median of 37.3x (P53) and the forward P/E is 25.1x, which makes it fair, but a P/B of 4.5x against a 10.6% ROE is rich, and the biggest risk is sell-side FY EPS estimates being cut 11–13% over 90 days while 33 of 37 analysts still rate it a buy, a classic pre-derating pattern.

ONGC is India's largest upstream oil and gas producer, so its earnings move with crude and gas prices, under a government-set policy framework (Energy sector card). The latest trend table stops at FY26, when revenue fell 3.9% to ₹132,508 cr and PAT fell 7.6% to ₹32,894 cr. However, the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 show a sharp turn: standalone Q2 PAT of ₹15,489 cr is about +57% versus roughly ₹9,848 cr in Q2 FY26, and H1 PAT of ₹32,522 cr is about +82% versus ₹17,872 cr, mainly because crude is higher. Quarterly revenue was not available from the filings, and the yfinance Q1 row (₹1.64L cr revenue) is consolidated and includes the refining subsidiaries, so it is not comparable. On valuation, I used P/E and dividend yield as the sector card advises for state-owned upstream companies: trailing P/E of 8.0x (forward 6.1x) and EV/EBITDA of 4.6x sit inside the card's 6–10x policy-priced band and slightly below the peer median of 9.2x (P33 on P/E, P17 on P/B at 0.9x). That makes it fair rather than cheap, because the discount reflects lasting policy risk. The yfinance dividend yield of 699% is clearly a data error and I ignored it. The biggest risk is that the government takes back the crude windfall through a windfall tax, subsidy sharing or a gas-price cap. Analysts have cut next-year EPS estimates by 3.6% over 90 days, which suggests they expect profits to fall back.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finserv is a financial-services holding company. Its value comes mainly from its 51.3% stake in Bajaj Finance (AUM ₹5,84,624 cr, up 26%), plus its life insurance, general insurance, housing finance and AMC businesses. In H1 FY27, consolidated revenue grew 17.9% YoY to ₹85,453 cr and PAT grew 21.6% to ₹12,249 cr. That is a pickup from +11.8% revenue growth in H1 FY26, though the half-year figures imply Q2 alone grew a slower ~15-16% after Q1's +19.2%. Lending quality keeps improving: Bajaj Finance's gross NPA fell from 1.24% to 1.06% YoY, net NPA from 0.60% to 0.42%, and life insurance VNB rose 53% to ₹783 cr. The PAT margin jumped from about 6.5% in FY26 to 14.3%, which looks like a change in how PAT is defined rather than a real improvement, so we do not count it as margin expansion. For a lender-heavy holding company we graded valuation on P/B against ROE, not P/E. At 3.5x book for a 14.6% ROE, ranking P73 in its sector on both P/B and trailing P/E (28.2x vs a 17.5x median), the stock looks fair, leaning full. Two things argue against calling it expensive: the forward P/E of 18.7x implies earnings growth, and the stock sits low in its 52-week range (21%). No sum-of-the-parts holding-company discount data was provided. The main risks are general insurance underwriting, now loss-making (combined ratio 104.7%, PAT down 24%), and possible dilution from Bajaj Finance's ₹11,700 cr QIP plus ₹5,800 cr of promoter warrants.

Bajaj Holdings is a near debt-free holding company. Its earnings come mainly from its stakes in Bajaj Auto and Bajaj Finserv, through dividends and its share of their profits. Its investment portfolio is worth about ₹2.40L cr at market value against a cost of ₹21,371 cr. In H1FY27, reported revenue fell 20.1% YoY to ₹576 cr and consolidated PAT fell 6.7% to ₹4,845 cr, and the trend table shows revenue growth slowing from triple digits to negative. That headline is distorted: last year included a one-off ₹1,522 cr gain from selling Bajaj Finserv shares. Without it, PAT grew about 37% YoY, and the share of associate profits rose about 32% to ₹4,626 cr, helped by Bajaj Auto (+62% PAT in Q2) and Bajaj Finserv (+23%). For a holding company the right yardstick is the discount to NAV, not P/E or EV/EBITDA. The EV/EBITDA of 128x and the 157% dividend yield in the snapshot are artefacts of this structure, and the yield figure looks like a data error. The share price is about ₹10,300, about 28% of the way up its 52-week range, against a reported NAV of ₹21,578 per share. That is roughly a 52% discount, inside the 40–60% norm for Indian holding companies, so I grade it fair. That fits the P/B of 1.5x with a 12.6% ROE and the trailing P/E of 11.4x, which is in the bottom third of its sector. The biggest risk is concentration: value and earnings depend almost entirely on two Bajaj Group stocks. Reported results are also lumpy, with one-off stake sales, lower dividends from Bajaj Auto after its buyback, weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.40x, mostly because associate profits are not cash) and a pending RBI decision on CIC status.

fundamental.thesis: Supreme Industries is India's largest plastics processor, selling plastic pipes (including CPVC), industrial, packaging and consumer products through about 50,000 distributors. It is a building-materials and consumer-demand business, not an order-book capital-goods company, so the Industrials sector card fits it only loosely. The latest verified filing is the FY26 annual result: revenue of Rs 11,218 cr (+7.0% YoY) and PAT of Rs 954 cr (-1.0% YoY), with an 8.5% PAT margin. Volumes grew 12% and piping volumes 14%, beating an industry that shrank 9%, but piping value grew only 11%, so falling PVC prices are eating into growth. Profit has not kept pace with volume, and Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 filings are not indexed (Q2 results come out today), so the trajectory cannot be confirmed. On valuation (EV/EBITDA and peer rank), the trailing P/E of 47x is above the static 28-45x Industrials band but 12.6% below the live peer median of 53.8x (P38). EV/EBITDA of 29.5x is 13% below the peer median (P41), and the stock sits at 27% of its 52-week range, which adds up to fair rather than cheap. The 99% dividend yield and the 1.47 debt/equity in the snapshot look like data errors and were not used. The biggest risk is that today's Q2 print confirms continued margin pressure, with sell-side FY EPS estimates already cut 2% over 90 days.

Dixon Technologies is India's largest contract electronics maker (EMS). It assembles smartphones, TVs, lighting, IT hardware and telecom gear, and is building camera-module and display capacity under the PLI scheme and the China+1 shift. The filed H1 FY27 figures show revenue of ₹37,938 cr and PAT of ₹1,129 cr, with PAT up 51% YoY. That leaves an implied Q2 of about ₹21,900–22,400 cr revenue and ₹411–466 cr PAT, which is only about a 2% PAT margin against 4.3–4.5% in Q1 FY27. Q1 revenue grew +21% to +25% (the two extracted Q1 rows disagree). The reported +147% H1 revenue growth and the ₹4,959 cr FY26 row do not reconcile with the quarterly figures, so the growth rate cannot be trusted. Margins are being diluted as volume grows faster than profit. Because this is an assembly-heavy, low-margin business, I graded on EV/EBITDA plus trailing P/E. EV/EBITDA is 32.3x, and trailing P/E of 42.9x sits at the top of the 28–45x Industrials range, so I grade it fair-to-full rather than cheap even though the stock is only 22% up its 52-week range. The peer-rank block compares Dixon with IT-services companies (WIPRO, INFY, PERSISTENT), which are not real peers, so I gave its 'P100 expensive' verdict little weight. The forward P/E is above the trailing P/E, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 7% over 30 days and 10% over 90 days while ratings stay 22 buy. That pattern often comes before a de-rating. FY26 cash conversion was also weak: cash from operations was only 0.22x PAT and free cash flow was -₹271 cr.

Thermax is a mid-cap Industrials company that makes energy and environment equipment (boilers, heating, cooling, water and air treatment, green energy). Its revenue comes mostly from working through its order book, and it is well placed for the capex and decarbonisation cycle. Revenue growth sped up from -5.4% (Q2FY26) to +6.7% (Q1FY27) to +11.4% in Q2FY27, at Rs 2,756 cr, but profit has not kept up. Consolidated PAT fell 5% YoY to Rs 113 cr, a PAT margin of 4.1% against 4.8% a year ago, hurt by product mix, input-cost inflation and a Rs 15 cr impairment in Green Solutions. Order booking fell 8% YoY to Rs 3,259 cr, the second straight quarterly decline. The backlog of Rs 14,250 cr (+16%) covers only about 1.3x trailing revenue, well below the 3x level that gives multi-year visibility. Using EV/EBITDA, the right measure for an order-book capital-goods business, the stock trades at 53.5x versus a peer median of 34.0x (P82). Trailing P/E of 76x and forward P/E of 50x (P82) are both above the 28-45x sector band, and the stock sits at 91% of its 52-week range, so it is expensive. The biggest risk is that profit keeps lagging revenue while order inflow weakens. FY EPS estimates have already been cut 17.6% over 90 days, which leaves this premium multiple open to a de-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. That makes it a high-beta bet on market activity, not a lender. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. For a fee-based broker I graded on P/E cross-checked with P/B against ROE: trailing P/E of 35.8x is above the 18–28x NBFC/capital-markets band and in line with the broad market (P52), while forward P/E of 20.3x prices in a further earnings recovery. P/B of 5.25x against only 15.5% ROE is rich, so overall this is fair at best, with the stock at 97% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 3.5% in 30 days and 4.8% in 90 days. The biggest risk is regulatory: further SEBI tightening of retail F&O, or a drop in market activity in this risk-off tape, would hit volumes directly. Cash flow from operations was also deeply negative in FY26 (-4.5x PAT) because the borrowed-money margin-funding book grew about 39%, which adds leverage (debt/equity about 1.0–1.3x).

Astral makes plumbing pipes and fittings, and also sells paints and adhesives. The desk tags it as Industrials, but it behaves more like a building-materials franchise, and plumbing brings in most of its revenue and most of its margin. In H1 FY27, revenue grew 21.4% YoY to ₹3,566 cr: plumbing rose 18.2% at a 12.9% segment margin and paints & adhesives rose 29.0%, but that segment's margin is only about 3.1%. PAT grew more slowly, up 15.7% to ₹248 cr (6.9% margin), and operating cash flow swung to -₹68 cr from +₹389 cr a year ago because of a large tax outflow, inventory build-up and 29% higher capex. The prior-period rows in the trend table are clearly wrong (for example, Q4FY26 revenue of ₹17,347 cr), so there is no reliable multi-quarter trend to rely on. On the sector card's preferred yardstick, EV/EBITDA is 35.7×, about 5% above the peer median of 34.0× (P59). Trailing P/E is 68.2× against a peer median of 53.8× (P62), and forward P/E is 43.3×, which already prices in earnings growth. That makes the stock fairly valued: there is no clear mispricing, though it sits at 32% of its 52-week range, which is a reasonable but not compelling entry point. The biggest risk is quality of growth. Profit is lagging revenue, cash conversion turned negative, paints is a low-margin segment, and the ₹95 mn goodwill impairment on Seal It (US) shows past acquisitions have not all paid off.

fundamental.thesis: GIC Re is India's dominant state-owned reinsurer. It takes on risk from domestic insurers across fire, motor, health, agriculture and other lines, and AM Best rates it A- (Excellent) with a stable outlook. In H1 FY27, gross written premium grew 11.7% year on year to ₹24,713 cr, faster than the +5.8% to +6.4% of FY26 and H1 FY26. Profit fell the other way: consolidated PAT dropped 12.8% to ₹4,709 cr, PAT margin shrank from 26.8% to 19.1%, and the combined ratio worsened slightly from 106.36% to 106.79%. That means the company loses money on underwriting and relies on ₹5,015 cr of investment income. Q2 alone (about ₹2,966 cr of PAT, implied by H1 minus Q1) was much better than Q1, whose PAT fell 31%. For an insurer I grade value on price-to-book against ROE, not P/E. At 0.62x book, the cheapest in the peer set and near the bottom of its 52-week range, the stock is cheap even for a below-par 9.1% ROE, and the 4.18x solvency ratio gives a large capital buffer. The trailing P/E of 6.8x supports this but is not my yardstick. The ROE gap is the main reason the market keeps this PSU at a discount to book. The biggest risk is that underwriting losses stay above 100% of premium while estimates keep being cut (FY EPS down 10% over 90 days), so earnings would depend on volatile investment gains.

fundamental.thesis: Choice International is a mid-sized diversified financial services group. Broking is about 59% of revenue, government and IPO advisory about 27%, and a small NBFC lending arm about 13%; it has 13.78 lakh demat accounts (+14% YoY) and ₹66,300 cr of client assets. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 35.9% YoY to ₹373 cr, up from +32-34% in Q1 and +16.6% a year earlier, so growth is speeding up. Profit is not keeping pace: PAT grew only 23.0% to ₹70 cr, the PAT margin slipped to 18.3% (19.6% in Q1, 20.5% a year ago) and EBITDA margin eased from 35.8% to 34.5%. I graded valuation on P/B against ROE, the yardstick for lenders and brokers rather than P/E: a P/B of 8.4x for a 16.2% ROE is expensive (P74 vs the broad market), and the trailing P/E of 63x (P80) is well above the 18-28x NBFC range. A forward P/E of 47x shows the market already expects strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that much of this business rises and falls with market activity, so a slowdown in broking volumes or IPO deals would hit growth that is already fully priced in, while the bonus issue and two fresh acquisitions add integration and accounting noise.

Valuation is fair: the sector card names no yardstick for this non-lending model, so I used trailing P/E of 45.2x (P66, +28% vs the broad-market median of 35.2x) and EV/EBITDA of 27.3x (P60, +17% vs 23.3x), with P/B of 9.4x (P79) partly backed by 22.3% ROE, the stock at 20% of its 52-week range, and a forward P/E of 32.2x that already assumes solid earnings growth. Authum Investment & Infrastructure is a mid-cap NBFC and investment holding company. Its earnings come mainly from gains on its investment portfolio and from buying distressed assets through the insolvency (NCLT) process, so profits swing a lot from quarter to quarter. It does not run a steady lending book. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 12.6% YoY to ₹685 cr, but PAT fell 45.5% YoY to ₹418 cr and PAT margin dropped to 61.0% from 74.6% in Q1. Revenue growth has also slowed, from +21.4% in Q1 to +12.6%. H1FY27 cash flow from operations was negative at -0.49x PAT, which means reported profits are not turning into cash. For a lender or holding company, P/B against ROE is the right yardstick, not P/E. On that basis the stock is fair rather than cheap: P/B is 2.91x for an ROE of 13.1%, well above the 'cheap' bar of P/B under 1.5 with ROE over 12%. The headline trailing P/E of 8.95x, in the bottom 5% of the market, overstates how cheap it is because it rests on large investment gains that may not repeat. The biggest risk is that earnings depend on market-linked investment gains and lumpy distressed-asset deals, and profits are not backed by cash. Leverage is also unclear: the live snapshot shows debt/equity of 24.59, which is unverified and could be a percentage misread.

Bharti Airtel is India's number-two telecom operator by revenue share (about 33%) and the main pure play on rising prices per user, with extra growth from Airtel Africa, Indus Towers, home broadband and enterprise. In Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue grew 16.7% YoY to 6,088 and net profit grew 30.8% YoY to 889, giving a 14.6% PAT margin and a stable 57.9% EBITDA margin; India mobile ARPU rose to Rs 271 (+5.9% YoY) from Rs 257–259 over the prior two quarters. Using EV/EBITDA, the measure the sector card sets for telecom, the stock trades at 10.5×, inside the 9–12× norm for Indian mobile and around the 12th percentile versus the broad market. That makes it fair, not cheap, even though trailing P/E is 40.7×; forward P/E is 21.6×, net debt/EBITDA has improved to 1.18× from 1.63×, and the price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range (15%), which is a reasonable entry point. The main risk is that ARPU growth stays in mid-single digits without a fresh tariff hike, while capex stays high (~25% of revenue, with the Homes and Digital TV segments under margin pressure) and full-year EPS estimates have been cut 1.5% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Delhivery is India's largest independent third-party logistics company, earning most of its money from express parcel delivery for e-commerce and from part-truckload (PTL) freight, and it is not an order-book business. fundamental.thesis: IRB Infrastructure is India's largest private toll-road operator and developer. fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

Jain Resource Recycling is a non-ferrous metal recycler that makes copper, lead and aluminium from scrap. It is a commodity-spread business, recently listed, and copper is now about two-thirds of its revenue. Revenue is growing fast, but much of that comes from copper prices and profit is not keeping up. H1 FY27 revenue rose 65.5% YoY to ₹6,061 cr while PAT rose only 3.1% to ₹160 cr. Taking Q1 out of H1 suggests Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹3,337 cr (around +58% YoY, slower than Q1's +75.9%) and PAT of about ₹91 cr, which is roughly 8% lower than a year ago. EBITDA margin has fallen from 7.0% (9M FY26) to 5.7% (Q1) to 4.5% (H1), and PAT margin from 4.4% to about 2.7%. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because the sector card says to judge cyclical, commodity-spread businesses that way. On that measure the stock looks expensive. EV/EBITDA is 25.1×, against roughly 5–8× for cyclicals at mid-cycle, and trailing P/E is 35.8×, against a 12–22× Materials benchmark. The 19.9× forward P/E depends on earnings growth, but analysts have cut those estimates by about 19% over the last 90 days. The biggest risk is that margins keep shrinking while net debt is high (about 3.3× EBITDA, debt/equity about 82%). If copper prices or recycling spreads reverse, earnings could fall sharply.

fundamental.thesis: Chambal Fertilizers is one of India's largest private urea makers. It also sells traded and complex fertilisers and crop-protection products, and it has just started a new Technical Ammonium Nitrate (TAN) plant at Gadepan from August 20, 2026. Its earnings depend heavily on the government subsidy rules (New Urea Policy 2015 and NBS). Growth is going the wrong way: Q1FY27 revenue was ₹5,027 cr, down 11.8% YoY, and PAT was ₹524 cr, down 4.6%, after FY26 grew 25% on traded complex fertilisers. Q2FY27 PAT margin slipped to about 9.0% from 10.4% in Q1, but the Q2 revenue figure was not extracted from the filing and the yfinance quarterly rows (Q2 revenue ₹4,367 cr) do not match the PDF figures, so the latest-quarter picture is only partly confirmed. I graded this as a capital-intensive commodity business on EV/EBITDA, which at 7.3x sits at the low end of the 5–8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals. Trailing P/E of 9.9x is below the 12–22x Materials benchmark, ROE is 20.5%, net debt is slightly negative (the 10.27 'debt/equity' looks like a percentage, given 48x interest coverage), and the stock is in the bottom decile of the broad market on every multiple, so the verdict is cheap. Cash conversion is the biggest worry: FY26 operating cash flow covered only 0.07x of PAT and receivables jumped from ₹368 cr to ₹2,075 cr, which looks like delayed subsidy payments and makes the reported earnings less solid than they appear.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Ingrevia is a mid-cap Indian chemicals maker with three segments: Specialty Chemicals, Nutrition (vitamin B3 and feed premixes) and Chemical Intermediates (acetyls). It is now adding CDMO capacity and has bought a 40% stake in ZettaOne, an electronics-materials business. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹1,394 cr, up 24% YoY and an all-time high, compared with low-single-digit growth through FY26 (+1.3% in Q1FY26, +5.0% for FY26). PAT rose 61% to ₹111 cr, and both PAT margin (8.0% vs 6.1–7.2% across FY26) and EBITDA margin (16.0% vs 13.6–14.8%) widened, but Q1FY27 is missing from the filings data, so the speed-up rests mainly on one quarter. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, as the sector card says to for chemicals: at 18.1x it is far above the card's 5–8x mid-cycle range for commodity chemicals, though that range doesn't fully fit a specialty/CDMO mix; it is 22% below the broad-market median (P35), with trailing P/E of 34.6x at P48 and forward P/E of 22.3x, so I call it fair overall, not cheap. The main risks are muddy cash flow and earnings quality: finance costs jumped 85% YoY on acquisition-related borrowing, H1 FY26 earnings were weakly backed by cash (0.67x CFO/PAT, negative free cash flow), and analysts have trimmed next-year EPS estimates (−2.4% over 30 days, −3.7% over 90 days) even as they raised this year's.

fundamental.thesis: Linde India is a subsidiary of the global Linde group that makes industrial gases and also runs a lower-margin project engineering arm. Gases bring in about 71% of segment revenue at a 26.4% segment margin, while project engineering earns only 9.8%. The latest extracted quarter, Q1FY27, shows revenue of ₹694 cr, up 21.6% YoY, but PAT fell 2.4% YoY to ₹105 cr. PAT margin has slipped to 15.1% from the low-to-mid 20s in earlier periods, and the H1 EBITDA margin dropped 850 bps to 31.8%. In short, sales are growing faster but that growth is not reaching profit, and heavy capex (about 96% of H1 revenue) pushed free cash flow to -₹647 cr. Industrial gases is a utility-like business, not a steel or cement cyclical, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and peer multiples. EV/EBITDA was not available, so I fell back on peer multiples: trailing P/E of 99.6x, forward P/E of 73.8x and P/B of 12.7x put it at P93/P98/P89 against the broad market, roughly 180-220% above the median, which is clearly expensive. Sell-side next-year EPS estimates have been cut about 14% over the last 30-90 days. The Q2FY27 results (filed 3 Nov) have not been extracted yet, so this view rests on Q1 and H1 data.

fundamental.thesis: Concord Biotech is a midcap maker of fermentation-based pharma ingredients and formulations, with low debt (debt/equity 0.12), though this pack does not contain enough data to judge its market position. Revenue growth has swung from -20.3% in Q2 FY26 to +26.2% in Q1 FY27 and about +25% in Q2 FY27 (derived as H1 Rs 567 cr less Q1 Rs 257 cr, or about Rs 310 cr), but this is an easy-base recovery: Q2 revenue is only back to roughly its Q2 FY25 level, implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 68 cr is up only about 7% YoY, and implied EBITDA margin has fallen to about 29% from 36.7%, while H1 cash conversion stayed healthy at 1.32x CFO/PAT. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick, cross-checked with P/E because no tight listed peers were available, the stock looks expensive at 37.0x EV/EBITDA (P78 and 59% above the broad-market median) and 50.8x trailing P/E against a 28-40x pharma range; the 34.4x forward P/E already prices in a strong profit recovery, and the +23.8% sell-side upside looks unreliable because the Rs 1,520 mean target is only about 5% above the roughly Rs 1,450 price implied by market cap and EPS. The biggest risk is that profit does not catch up with revenue, since FY27 EPS estimates were cut 2.8% in the last 30 days and the valuation leaves little room for further margin slippage; confidence is also limited because the FY26 revenue and PAT rows appear overstated tenfold, the 51% dividend yield is clearly wrong, and no sector KPIs or management guidance were available.

Anthem Biosciences is a contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) company with a smaller specialty-ingredients arm; CRDMO made up 84% of H1 FY27 revenue. It has a clean record with regulators (USFDA, TGA, ANVISA), net cash of ₹1,538 cr, and FY26 cash flow of 1.48x PAT. Revenue has gone from +15.0% growth in FY26 to a -7.2% fall in H1 FY27 (₹1,012 cr). Q1 fell 22.6% to ₹418 cr. Q2 recovered to about ₹594 cr, roughly +8% YoY, a figure we worked out from the H1 and Q1 numbers. H1 PAT rose 7.2% to ₹331 cr, a 30.2% margin, but part of that margin comes from other income booked inside EBITDA (₹84 cr, about 17% of EBITDA). We graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the measure the sector card favours for capital-heavy CDMO businesses. At 50.8x EV/EBITDA and 76x trailing P/E, the stock is far above the 28–40x pharma P/E range and sits around P86–P93 against peers on every multiple, so it is expensive even allowing a China+1 CDMO premium. The analyst mean target is only 0.7% above the current price, and next-year earnings estimates have been cut 3.6% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Pharmova is a diversified Indian pharma company spanning CDMO Sterile Injectables, Allergy Immunotherapy, Radiopharma, and Generics — a complex, multi-segment business with meaningful US and Canada exposure. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue accelerated to +17.3% YoY (₹2,229 cr), continuing a multi-quarter re-acceleration from +9.8% in Q1FY26, but PAT collapsed 45% YoY to ₹56 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from 15.9% (Q1FY26) to 12.0%, with CDMO Sterile Injectables margins imploding from 11% to 1.4% and the Generics segment swinging to a ₹10 cr operating loss — a dangerous divergence between topline and bottom-line trajectories. Trailing P/E of 38.8× sits near the top of the pharma sector benchmark range (28–40×) on deeply-depressed earnings; EV/EBITDA of 14.17× (P23 percentile vs broad peers) looks more attractive but still reflects deteriorating EBITDA; forward P/E of 19.16× embeds a steep earnings recovery that consensus has already cut by ~25% in the last 30 days, making the 'cheap-on-forward' narrative fragile. The biggest risk is a dual FDA compliance overhang — OAI at Montreal (remediation expenses of ₹535 mn already booked, manufacturing suspended) plus a live USFDA Spokane update — alongside a GST show-cause notice and a high debt/equity ratio (50.94×), any one of which could derail the assumed margin recovery.

Lloyds Metals and Energy is a fast-growing midcap that mines iron ore and makes pellets and sponge iron (DRI). It is in the middle of a heavy capacity build-out, so its earnings swing with iron-ore and steel spreads. Subtracting Q1FY27 from H1FY27 (₹13,009 cr revenue, ₹2,791 cr PAT) gives Q2FY27 revenue of about ₹5,655 cr (+52.5% YoY vs ₹3,707 cr) and PAT of about ₹1,057 cr (+86% YoY vs ₹567 cr). But revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +204.5% in Q3FY26 and +208.6% in Q1FY27 to +52.5%. Revenue fell about 23% and PAT about 39% from Q1, partly due to the monsoon season, and PAT margin dropped from 23.6% to about 18.7%. Using EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cyclical, the stock trades at 19.1×, far above the 5–8× mid-cycle norm for steel and mining names. Trailing P/E of 26.3× is also above the 12–22× Materials range, so I grade it expensive. The 12.1× forward P/E and analysts' +38% upgrades to FY earnings estimates only hold up if the new capacity delivers on time, and the stock is already at 84% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt/equity of about 1.45×, FY26 free cash flow of -₹1,853 cr and fresh NCD (bond) raises mean any delay in commissioning or a fall in iron-ore prices would hurt both earnings and the leverage story.

fundamental.thesis: Max Healthcare is one of India's largest listed hospital chains, with about 6,100 network beds running at more than 75% occupancy. It is growing by adding beds at existing hospitals and buying new ones (Kalinga in Bhubaneswar, a land parcel in Pune, 85 more beds at its Noida hospital). Taking H1 FY27 minus Q1, Q2 FY27 revenue comes to about ₹2,569 cr, up about 20% YoY, and EBITDA margin has widened from 26.8% to 28.2% over the trend window. But revenue growth has slowed from above 30% to about 17–20%, and H1 PAT fell 7.7% YoY to ₹737 cr. Most of that fall comes from the tax rate going back to normal: it rose from an unusually low 5.6% to 24.5% because of a one-off merger-related tax reversal last year. Cash generation is solid, with operating cash flow at 1.35x PAT and ₹406 cr of free cash flow in H1. Because hospitals are capital-heavy, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, which is 45.6x, about 96% above the broad-market median (P86). Trailing P/E is 73.9x against a 35.2x median (P85), and P/B is 9.9x for only a 14.3% ROE, so the stock is expensive even with forward P/E falling to 44.9x. The biggest risk is that analysts keep cutting their EPS estimates (down 4.5% over 90 days) while capex for new beds and acquisitions stays heavy. That could lead to a de-rating even though 21 of 28 analysts still rate it a buy. Two numbers don't line up: the press release reports Q2 revenue of ₹3,219 cr and PAT of ₹448 cr (+10%), likely on a gross or network basis, while the trend table implies ₹2,569 cr and ₹414 cr. Also, the 15% dividend yield and 32.37 debt/equity in the snapshot look like data errors and were ignored.

fundamental.thesis: Neuland Laboratories makes APIs (active drug ingredients) and does contract development and manufacturing (CDMO) for global drugmakers. About 85% of revenue comes from exports, and it has 77 active US drug master files (DMFs) and a clean FDA record. It should benefit from the China+1 shift, and its export-led model is outside the US tariff on patented drugs. Results are lumpy, though: Q2FY27 revenue fell 11.4% YoY to ₹457 cr and PAT fell 47% to ₹51 cr. That came straight after an exceptional Q1 (revenue +116%, PAT ₹147 cr), and the PAT margin dropped from 22.7% to 11.2% between the two quarters. H1FY27 still looks strong, with revenue up 35% to ₹1,091 cr, PAT up 80% to ₹199 cr and cash flow from operations at 1.8x PAT. On valuation I used trailing and forward P/E and P/B, because the reported EV/EBITDA of 401x and debt/equity of 16x are almost certainly data errors for a company the filings show as net cash. At 60.6x trailing earnings (sector range 28–40x), 11.8x book and the P78 peer percentile, the stock is expensive. The 37.6x forward P/E already assumes the H1 growth rate carries on. The biggest risk is that the Q2 drop marks a pause in big customer orders rather than normal quarter-to-quarter swings, which would leave a premium valuation without the earnings to support it.

P/E (36.8×, in line with the market median) and EV/EBITDA (negative) are both distorted by the tax credit and the weak EBITDA, so I graded on P/B plus ROE: 1.42× book is low for the broad market (P9) but matches a 3% ROE, so fair, not cheap; on underlying earnings the stock is effectively loss-making, and the price sitting near its 52-week low (10% of range) looks more like a falling knife than value. The biggest risk is leverage: net debt is ₹1,471 cr, about 7.3× annualised EBITDA, and the promoter pledged more shares again in October and November 2026.

The biggest risk is that cost pressures (crude rising, competitive intensity in RAC) persist through FY27, making the earnings recovery priced into the forward multiple elusive and triggering a de-rating in a premium-multiple name where any guidance miss historically compresses valuation 25–40%.

The biggest structural risk is that Pizza Hut's decline deepens post-merger integration while high finance costs (₹70 cr/quarter, 4.4% of revenue) keep PAT margins razor-thin, with sell-side EPS estimates already revised down -8.4% over 90 days despite a still-bullish analyst mix — a classic pre-derating pattern.

Bata India is India's largest footwear retailer, with about 2,000 stores and a growing franchise network. It is a mass-to-mid-market brand in a K-shaped consumer market where premium players are taking share. The trend has not recovered convincingly: Q1FY27 revenue was ₹979 cr (+4.0% YoY), only a modest pickup after five periods of flat-to-negative growth (FY26 +0.6%, H1FY26 -2.2%). FY26 PAT fell 59.5% to ₹134 cr, a 3.8% margin, partly because of ₹42 cr of VRS costs. VRS costs continued in H1FY27 (₹13 cr) along with a ₹5.8 cr forex loss, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-03 are not yet in the extracted data. Franchisee like-for-like growth in the high single digits is the one positive KPI. I graded valuation on P/E plus ROE, because the low 13.7× EV/EBITDA is inflated by lease accounting. On that basis the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E is 75.6× (P86 vs the broad market, +115% vs the 35× median) and P/B is 6.4× on an ROE of only 8.5%. That is a premium-retailer multiple for a business growing revenue in low single digits. The forward P/E of 37× assumes a profit recovery that has not shown up yet. Sell-side views are bearish (8 sell out of 14), and FY EPS estimates have been cut 8.2% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the margin recovery story keeps slipping while estimates keep being cut, which would push the multiple down further.

fundamental.thesis: Lemon Tree Hotels owns and manages hotels and is expanding through brand-licence and franchise signings, including an MoU with Omaxe for about 4,000 keys, while a pending demerger would separate hotel ownership from the management and brand businesses. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 16.07x is 31% below the broad-market median (P29) and the stock is near its 52-week low at 15.1% of the range, but with no hotel peer set or card-specific norm and a 39x trailing P/E (P56), I grade it fair rather than cheap. The 22x forward P/E assumes about 77% EPS growth over the trailing base, which looks demanding against 19-21% recent profit growth and FY estimates cut 5.8% over 90 days despite 21 of 22 analysts rating it a buy, and Q2 FY27 results on 2026-11-05 will test this with no RevPAR or management guidance data available here.

fundamental.thesis: PVR INOX is a leading Indian multiplex operator whose results depend on film releases and cinema footfall, and it sold its Zea Maize food business in January 2026. H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

TBO Tek runs a B2B travel-distribution platform that connects travel agents worldwide to hotel and airline inventory, and since the Classic Vacations acquisition it also has a North American leisure arm. In Q2FY27 reported revenue of ₹866 cr grew 52.5% YoY, slower than Q1's +81%, and most of that headline growth comes from the acquisition: organic GTV grew 22% and organic gross profit 21%, while organic adjusted EBITDA grew 36%. Consolidated EBITDA margin has contracted from 22.5% to 17.6% over the trend window, and the last PAT margin we have is 9.0% in Q1FY27, down from about 14% a year earlier, because the lower-margin Classic Vacations business now makes up more of the mix. Q2 PAT was not available from the filings, and the revenue scale in the trend table does not match the yfinance rows, so treat the absolute figures with some caution. On valuation, the sector card says platform names should be judged on EV/EBITDA and growth delivery, not P/E alone: at 39.3x EV/EBITDA (P81 vs the broad market) and 68.4x trailing P/E (P83), with the stock at 88.8% of its 52-week range, the shares look expensive even though the forward P/E of 33.5x assumes strong earnings growth. The biggest risk is that the price assumes perfection while FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days and governance issues are piling up: an unprovisioned ED/FEMA penalty of about ₹22 cr, an ₹8.1 cr employee fraud at an overseas subsidiary, and ₹8.9 cr of FX losses.

fundamental.thesis: Endurance Technologies makes auto parts, mainly for two-wheelers in India, including suspension, braking, transmission and aluminium castings. About 76% of its H1 revenue came from India and 24% from its plants in Italy and Germany. In H1FY27, revenue grew +31.6% YoY to ₹9,159 cr and PAT grew +14.4% to ₹519 cr. Taking H1 minus Q1 gives an implied Q2 revenue of about ₹4,811 cr (+33.5% YoY, up from +29.6% in Q1) and PAT of about ₹274 cr (+21% YoY, up from +8% in Q1). Profits are growing much more slowly than sales, though. EBITDA margin fell from 13.1% in Q1 to about 12.1% in Q2, PAT margin is stuck near 5.6–5.7%, and analysts cut their FY earnings estimates by 4% over the last 90 days. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 39.4x is above the 18–30x auto range and the 18–28x auto-ancillary range. But the forward P/E of 26.4x sits inside that range, and EV/EBITDA of 18.7x is below the broad-market median of 23.3x, so overall the stock is fair, with no margin of safety. The biggest risk is that the very strong sales growth keeps failing to lift profit margins while estimates keep getting cut, which would squeeze the premium the stock trades at.

fundamental.thesis: ABFRL is a midcap fashion retailer that owns Pantaloons (value retail, 399 stores), an ethnic-wear portfolio including TCNS and Jaypore, the TMRW digital brands and a small luxury arm, with about 1,286 stores in total. Revenue growth has slowed from about +11% YoY in Q1 FY27 (₹2,026 cr) to +6.4% for H1 FY27 (₹4,056 cr), so Q2 grew only about 2% YoY (Q2 revenue ≈ ₹2,030 cr, worked out from H1 minus Q1). Losses got worse: Q2 PAT was about ₹-376 cr, a margin of about -18.5%, against -12.3% in Q1. H1 EBITDA fell 28% YoY to ₹130 cr, and free cash flow was ₹-288 cr. The business is loss-making, so P/E means nothing here; I graded on EV/EBITDA and P/B. EV/EBITDA is 18.2x, against 23.3x for the broad-market median (P36). P/B is 1.28x (P7), which looks cheap, but return on equity is -12.7%, so we call valuation fair, not cheap, even though the stock sits near its 52-week low (19% of range). The biggest risk is that the turnaround keeps failing: no segment makes money at the profit line, the ethnic segment's margin is -23%, and net debt of ₹1,334 cr is about 10x EBITDA.

fundamental.thesis: Motherson Sumi Wiring India makes wiring harnesses for Indian carmakers and two-wheeler makers, and its sales depend mostly on Indian volumes, which makes it a direct play on India's premium-vehicle and EV mix. The profit margin fell from 6.0% to 4.3% and the operating margin from 10.2% to 7.7%. There are early signs of a recovery: the half-year filing implies Q2 profit of about Rs 224 cr (+35% YoY, which matches yfinance's Rs 223 cr), FY EPS estimates were raised +7.3% in the last 30 days, and the half-year revenue figure is labelled H1FY26 in the table but is probably H1 FY27. However, the 30 Oct Q2 FY27 results have not been extracted yet and the Q2 revenue figures conflict, so this recovery is unconfirmed. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA and forward P/E, as the Auto card suggests for ancillaries: EV/EBITDA of 23.9x is at the peer median (P52), forward P/E of 25.1x sits inside the 18-30x Auto band, and trailing P/E of 40.2x is inflated by the margin dip. That makes the stock fair, not cheap, even though it trades near its 52-week low (11.5% of range) and has a 32.4% ROE. The 293% dividend yield and 10.79 debt/equity readings look like data-unit errors; the filings show net debt of only Rs 58 cr. The biggest risk is that margins stay squeezed by copper and commodity costs, rising crude and a new-plant ramp-up, so revenue keeps growing without profit following it.
